column4: The section's dictionary form rabāba is a cloud with parts piled one over another; here clouds are joined and made rukāman before rain and hail descend.
The source's rabāb is a plant-nourishing cloud; this verse stages winds raising and spreading clouds until rain falls, then names the rain as mercy.
The source calls rabāb a cloud that nourishes plants; here winds drive clouds to a dead land, and rain gives it life again.
The prose itself names this rain after despair: people lose hope, then God sends al-ghayth and spreads mercy, making the cloud-and-growth image a renewal of provision.

The source's rabab family includes collected water and plants that stay green in summer; this verse traces rain into springs and growth, then yellowing and debris, showing both flourishing and its limit.
The source's n-h-r dictionary sense is an overflowing watercourse that cuts earth; this verse has torrents flowing through valleys, foam passing away, and what benefits remaining.
The source's rabāb is a cloud named for growing plants; here wind carries heavy clouds to a dead land, rain brings forth fruit, and the passage calls the wind a bearer of good news.
The source links blessing with the moist south wind; this verse describes fertilizing winds and water sent down from the sky, directly joining wind, water, and growth.
The source's secondary niʿma dictionary form is the wet southern wind; this verse has winds precede mercy and carry glad news of purifying water.
The water in this verse revives a dead land and gives drink to people and livestock, echoing the section's cloud nourishing soil and its rain-as-provision image.
The verse says people had despaired before rain came; that is the same reversal from withheld provision to mercy developed in the section's cited 42:28.
It asks the reader to see how God's mercy revives earth after its death; the rain-grown land makes the section's cloud and plant growth visible.
Lightning brings fear and hope, then rain revives dead earth; the verse gathers weather and renewed growth into one scene like the section's cloud over dry soil.
This verse joins alternating night and day, rain, winds, clouds held between sky and earth, and revived land, bringing together several stages of the section's image.
The source's rabāb is a cloud that nourishes plants; this verse brings water down and describes the resulting vegetation, grain, palms, grapes, and varied fruit.
The source links a nourishing cloud with plant growth; here rain is drink for people and water for vegetation and trees.
The verse names crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits grown by rain, giving a concrete catalogue of the nourishment carried by the section's cloud image.
The verse joins earth as a spread place, paths through it, water from the sky, and plants of different kinds; it stages the soil-and-rain relation behind the section's image.
After calling earth lifeless, the verse says rain makes it stir and grow every kind of lovely plant; it directly parallels the dead soil made fruitful by rain.
The source's n-h-r entry describes digging a well until water is reached; this verse says water is lodged in earth and can also be taken away, making access to it a gift with a limit.
The verse answers that God sends water from the sky and revives the earth after its death; it states the same rain-to-growth relation as the section.
Earth lies humbled until rain falls and it grows; this is a close parallel to the cloud nourishing plant life on dry ground.
Rain is sent down in due measure to revive a dead land; the measured provision makes explicit how water supports growth.
The source's rabāb is a plant-nourishing cloud; this verse calls the descending water blessed and links it with grain and gardens.
The verse continues the rain-grown scene with tall date palms bearing clustered fruit, a specific image of abundant plant growth.
The plants and fruit are described as provision for servants, and the verse adds that dead land is revived; it joins growth to sustenance as the section does.
Noah's promise of rain in abundance connects water from above with the section's image of gathered water that sustains growth.
The next verse names gardens and rivers after abundant rain; its own contribution is to show rain issuing in sustained provision.
The verse says God made people grow from earth like plants; this makes the section's plant-growing root image a direct metaphor for human nurture.
The verse brings water and pasture from the earth for people and livestock; it joins gathered water to plant and animal sustenance, as the section's secondary senses do.
The verse names trellised and untrellised gardens, dates, crops, and fruit; it gives a concrete scene of the earth yielding sustenance.
A grain grows into seven ears, each with many grains; the image makes multiplication through plant growth a picture of provision.
Fruit and date palms grow from the earth; this is a direct plant-bounty scene beside the section's cloud that nourishes vegetation.
The source's n-h-r entry is a river, and this verse makes a river the test of who may drink freely and who may take only a handful, turning abundant water into a measured boundary.
The flood scene opens the sky with pouring water; 54:12 completes it with springs bursting from earth and the waters meeting, an image of gathered abundance.
The earth releases springs and the waters meet, completing the sky-water deluge of 54:11; this is a concrete scene of abundant water gathering from above and below.
The verse promises abundant water to those who remain on the right path; it directly recalls the source's dictionary sense of collected, plentiful water.
The parable opens with two gardens of grapes, date palms, and crops; 18:33 adds their river, while this verse supplies the cultivated ground that water sustains.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner regrets his former boast; it shows cultivated abundance passing away, the boundary to the section's persistent cloud and summer-green plants.
The verse describes water poured down from clouds; in the next two ayat it yields grain, plants, and dense gardens, completing the rain-to-growth scene.
This verse names grain and plants as the result of the poured water in 78:14; it supplies the growth stage of the same scene.
It adds dense gardens to the rain-grown grain and plants of 78:14–15; the cited ayah's contribution is the abundance of the resulting vegetation.
The verse says water is poured down abundantly; 80:26–32 continue with split earth, grain, fruit, gardens, and pasture, while this ayah supplies the water source.
The source's n-h-r dictionary sense is a river cutting through earth; this verse says earth is split, and 80:25 and 80:27 show the water and crops around it.
This verse names grain growing from the split earth of 80:26; it gives a particular crop in the rain-and-growth sequence begun at 80:25.
Grapes and fodder continue the growth sequence after the grain of 80:27; they show the land yielding varied nourishment.
Olives and date palms extend the sequence of crops in 80:27–28, giving specific trees and fruits produced from the watered ground.
The verse adds enclosed gardens to the crop sequence in 80:27–29, showing plant abundance on a larger scale.
Fruit and pasture continue the garden scene of 80:30; the pasture also carries the growth image into food for animals.
This verse says the fruit and pasture are provision for people and livestock, connecting the growth sequence of 80:25–31 to the section's nourishment theme.
The verse calls the sky one of returning rain; 86:12 adds the earth splitting, joining recurring water above to opened ground below.
The source's n-h-r entry pictures water cutting earth; this verse gives the earth's split as the neighbour to the returning rain in 86:11.
After the years of famine in Joseph's interpretation, this ayah promises a year of rain and pressing produce; it makes provision return after want as in 42:28.
Hūd promises abundant rain and added strength if his people turn back; the rain is a direct sign of renewed provision.
The source describes a well dug until water is reached; here some stones split and rivers gush from them, turning hidden water into flowing abundance.
The source's n-h-r entry is an overflowing channel; this verse gives a garden scene with a river flowing between two cultivated plots.
The source names both rivers (n-h-r) and the abundant milk of a she-camel (s-j-w); this verse brings rivers of water and milk together in its garden scene.
The source's s-j-w dictionary note uses a she-camel whose milk becomes abundant; this verse describes drinkable milk produced by livestock.
The verse identifies milk among the benefits and drinks from livestock; it matches the source's secondary s-j-w sense of an animal whose milk is plentiful.
The prose explicitly notes this scene: Mary and her son are settled at a place of refuge with flowing water. The hill-name rabwa is only sound-similar to rabb, not the same root.
Mary's scene places a flowing stream below her at childbirth; alongside the refuge-and-water scene in 23:50, it makes water immediate provision in a vulnerable moment.
As the section notes, the same verse joins gardens with rivers and God's approval with the believers' approval; its river scene and mutual contentment connect water, reward, and satisfaction.
The verse joins rain sent from the sky, fruit as provision, and rivers made serviceable; it gathers the cloud, plant, and watercourse images into one account of provision.
The source's n-h-r entry names a river channel; this verse presents gardens with rivers beneath and fruits as provision, making the river part of a nourished landscape.
A garden of palms and grapes watered by a river is struck by a fiery whirlwind; the scene reverses the section's cloud that nourishes plants and shows how quickly provision can be lost.
The parable's good tree has a firm root and branches in the sky; it makes rooted growth visible in a section about a cloud nourishing plants.
The next ayah says the good tree yields fruit at all times by its Lord's leave; this fits the source's plant sense that does not wither in summer.
The bad tree is uprooted and has no stability, the reversal of the firmly rooted, fruitful tree in 14:24–25 and of the section's persistent green plants.
The promised garden has rivers, enduring food, and shade; the lasting provision gives a counter-image to the source's seasonal plants and their vulnerability to drying.
The source describes digging a well until water is reached; this ayah warns that garden water could sink into the ground and become unreachable, a direct reversal of finding water.
The verse asks who could bring springing water if it sank into earth; this reverses the source's well-digging image, where digging reaches water below.
The verse names a well left unused among ruined settlements; beside the source's well whose water has become abundant, it marks water's absence and lost habitation.
Rain-grown vegetation first flourishes, then dries and is scattered by wind; this gives a direct counterpart to the source's plants that do not wither in summer.
Rain makes the land flourish, then a night or day decree leaves it cut down as if it had not been; the verse sharpens the section's passing-and-lasting contrast.
Rain-grown crops turn yellow and become debris; this is a close image of flourishing that passes, set against the source's persistent cloud and summer-green plants.
The verse says God darkened the night and brought out its ḍuḥā; the source's first image glosses al-ḍuḥā as the cloudless sky, so this gives the bright counterpart to night.
This verse pairs night as repose with the splitting of dawn; it makes the night-to-day alternation in 93:1–2 part of an ordered cycle.
Night is a covering and sleep a rest, followed by day for rising; this parallels the still night and bright daytime stance of the section.
The verse calls night a covering; it supplies a direct image for the night that stands opposite the section's duha.
The day is made for livelihood, the counter-state to the covered night in 78:10 and a daylight counterpart to 93:1–2.
The oath describes night as it covers; this is a concise parallel to the night in 93:2.
The next oath describes day as it appears; its contribution is the revealed daytime that completes the night/day pair of 92:1 and 93:1–2.
The day is shown as it displays the sun; it gives another explicit bright daytime state to set beside the still night of the section.
The night covers the day in this verse, completing the paired alternation begun in 91:3 and matching 93:1–2's two opposed times.
This verse says people prefer the nearer life; alongside 93:4 and the section's transient, withering plant images, it identifies the preference for what passes.
It says the hereafter is better and more lasting; that permanence sharpens the section's contrast between lasting cloud or summer-green plants and what withers.

The verse concerns two orphan boys, a protected treasure, and their Lord's wish that they reach maturity; it makes the section's comparison between Rabb's plant-nourishing and care that lets an orphan grow concrete.
Orphans are tested until they reach marriageable maturity and sound judgment; the passage presents care as guiding them through growth, echoing the section's nurture image.
The righteous give food to an orphan and needy person; this makes nourishment an act of care for the vulnerable, parallel to the section's image of growth sustained by provision.
The verse names feeding an orphan who is a near kinsman; 90:14 sets this in a day of hunger, making material nourishment the specific link to the section's nurture of an orphan.
The next verse names a poor person in misery; its contribution after the orphan of 90:15 is the extension of nourishment to another vulnerable person.
The source explains Rabb through nourishing and raising; this prayer remembers parents who raised the speaker when small, using رَبَّيَانِي for nurture in another field.
Pharaoh says نُرَبِّكَ of raising Moses as a child; that same nurture sense helps make audible the section's comparison between the Lord growing plants and sheltering an orphan.

The garden owner is told to say “what God wills; no power except through God” on entering his garden; this makes the section's command to speak of the Lord's blessing concrete in a garden of provision.
At Midian, people water their flocks while two women hold theirs back; this joins the section's well-water and livestock-milk senses in one watering scene.
Moses draws water for the women's flock after the watering scene of 28:23; this adds water given to livestock, echoing the section's rain as provision for living things.
The verse describes pushing an orphan away, a clear opposite of 93:6's shelter and 93:9's protection, which the section reads through the image of nurture.
It condemns failing to urge feeding the poor; beside the orphan pushed away in 107:2, it reverses the section's image of provision that sustains growth.
The verse names grain and fragrant plants on earth; the next ayah asks which of the Lord's favors are denied, linking the section's plant growth and blessing to a concrete harvest.
The repeated question about the Lord's favors follows the grain and fragrant plants of 55:12; it resonates specifically with 93:11's command to speak of the Lord's blessing.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it; this is a specific reversal of 93:11's command to recount the Lord's blessing.
The source's secondary niʿma form is a moist, gentle south wind; this verse gives the opposite kind, a barren wind sent against a people and leaving nothing.

The garden owner's companion warns that a calamity from the sky could strike the garden; the cloud-bearing source that nourishes plants thus has a specific destructive boundary in this neighboring garden scene.
